metadata.title: Massive Texas backlog of voter registrations that scrambled workers has been cleared, state says

sources.news_title: Texas Says It Has Cleared a Massive Voter-Registration Backlog
sources.text:
By Anna Wilder
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — A massive backlog of voter registration applications in Texas that frustrated counties and raised concerns among Democrats nationally has been cleared days before early voting begins, state election officials said Thursday.
The backlog, which state officials attributed to a software glitch, left counties big and small scrambling to process scores of voter registrations late in an unusually competitive midterm election season in Texas. Early voting in the state begins Monday.
State officials have not said how many applications were delayed but the number was in the hundreds of thousands, including over 75,000 in Harris County, which includes Houston and finished its backlog earlier this month.
Trending
“With our size, that was a big win for our county,” said Harris County Tax Assessor and Voter Registrar Annette Ramirez, who oversees the county’s elections.
The problem, which officials in the Republican-controlled state have not publicly defined, started last October in the Texas Department of Public Safety, which among other things allows people to register to vote or update their voter registrations when they renew their driver’s license.
The error failed to send a large number of records to applicants’ home counties, where the applications are processed and verified. Those records could be a new voter registration application or an update to an existing registration, such as a change of address.
DPS had previously said certain records submitted online “were incomplete and not fully transmitted.” The department did not immediately respond to an email seeking further explanation Thursday.
Alicia Pierce, a spokeswoman for the Texas Secretary of State, said they were not aware of any county with pending applications. Her office has said that any person can still cast a provisional ballot if they show up to a polling place and are not on the voter rolls.
The League of Women Voters and the Texas Civic Fund, a civil rights group, filed a lawsuit that accused the state of not providing a reliable way for people to register to vote. California U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla, a Democrat and ranking member of the Senate Rules Committee that oversees federal elections, sent Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott a letter last month seeking answers on the scope of the failure and the causes.
Election offices hired temporary workers to handle the crush. In Austin, Travis County Tax Assessor Celia Israel said the backlog for her elections office was an “enhanced stress,” especially on top of seeing more voting applications coming in the last few weeks.

sources.news_title: Massive Texas backlog of voter registrations that scrambled workers has been cleared, state says
Local Texas election officials clear voter registration backlog caused by state error
Denton County election officials work to clear 42,000 voter registrations from DPS backlog before early voting
sources.text:
Nearly a month after the Texas Department of Public Safety discovered a software glitch that affected at least 200,000 voter registrations, the Denton County Elections Administration was still working earlier this week to clear about 2,500 out of the 42,000 registrations it received from the state on Sept. 23.
Elections Administrator Frank Phillips said Denton County’s software vendor was able to verify that a majority of the 42,000 registrations sent from DPS were already registered in the system, knocking the total down to 9,000 voter registrations still to process.
Phillips expects to have the registrations cleared before early voting begins Monday.
“There’s not a county in the state that wasn’t affected,” Phillips told the Denton Record-Chronicle on Tuesday.
Denton County Judge Andy Eads didn’t respond to a request for comment by Wednesday evening, but county spokesperson Dawn Cobb said the county was glad the state notified county election administrators across the state about DPS’ software issue.
“The County receives daily uploads from DPS and is working on the latest batches in the same way we do every day,” Cobb wrote in an email Wednesday. “Everything will be reconciled and ready for the election.”
DPS’ software glitch was due to an undisclosed error and affected records that Phillips said dated back to September 2025.
Discovered in late August, DPS indicated it was related to daily batch uploads of online driver’s license voter registration requests and that “certain online records were incomplete and not fully transmitted,” according to a Sept. 23 KXAN-TV report.
Phillips started working as an election administrator in 2009 and said he had never seen anything like this happen before with voter registrations. He pointed out that they get voter registration downloads from DPS every day.
Whenever the voter registrations come in, Phillips said they come in a different category that will tell him that this group of voters already exists in the system.
“I get the feeling that they didn’t know what they had sent and what they had not,” Phillips said. “And by they I mean DPS because thousands of these [voter registrations] already existed in our system.”
Phillips said that neighboring counties and other counties he spoke with had found the same thing. For example, Collin County, he said, had roughly 61,000 voter registrations from DPS and, similar to Denton County, knocked it down to 9,000.
Since the cutoff for voter registration in the May election, the county has received 39,797 new voter registration applications and 52,605 changes to existing applications from DPS and voter registration applications between April 3 and Oct. 5.
As long as a registration was received by Oct. 5, Phillips said the system will register them.
Phillips said the National Voter Registration Act of 1993 made it possible for people to register to vote at Department of Motor Vehicles locations across the nation.
“As a voter, I think it’s always safer to just fill out an old-school voter registration application,” Phillips said. “Now, if you’re already registered and you’re just changing your address, you can do that online at votetexas.gov. Then you don’t have to fill out the paper or worry about DPS.”

sources.news_title: Texas election officials clear voter registration backlog
sources.text:
This coverage is made possible through Votebeat, a nonpartisan news organization covering local election administration and voting access. Sign up for Votebeat Texas’ free newsletters here.
Election officials across Texas appear to have cleared a backlog of hundreds of thousands of voter registration applications and updates that went unprocessed for more than a year due to a state software error.
More than 500,000 voter registration records were caught in what the Texas Department of Public Safety said last month was an error related to a software update for the agency’s online driver’s license portal.
Roughly a month after state officials acknowledged the issue, The Texas Secretary of State’s Office and the Texas Association of County Election Officials both said on Wednesday that they’re not aware of any county still working through the backlog.
Kristin Miles, president of the election officials’ association and the Bastrop County election administrator, said the effort shows county election officials will do whatever it takes to ensure that eligible voters can cast ballots.
“If that means long nights and working weekends, county election officials are not going to fail the voters of Texas,” Miles said. But, she added, the state “should be looking at ways to prevent those things from happening again in the future to ensure that county election officials are not burdened by issues that may arise. Because at the end of the day, it was county election officials who put in the work to get the job done.”
Last month, Votebeat first reported on the backlogged voter registration records, which dated back to October 2025. The news came shortly before the state’s Oct. 5 voter registration deadline, which meant election officials had to scramble to get through backlogged records on top of hundreds of voter registration applications arriving daily.
Voting rights groups have sued the state, saying the backlog breached a 2021 settlement agreement that required Texas to provide a reliable way for people to register to vote through DPS’ online driver’s license portal.
Some better-resourced counties with outside vendors and additional technology, including Dallas, Harris, and Collin counties, were able to get through the backlog within a week. But many election officials said issues with the secretary of state’s voter registration system, known as TEAM, made the backlog harder to resolve during a critical time.
The Texas Secretary of State’s Office said it would offer counties grants to pay for costs related to the backlog, and on Wednesday confirmed it is still offering money to cover overtime and temporary workers.
“Texas counties have worked diligently and have cleared the backlog. We don’t know of any counties with pending applications,” Alicia Pierce, the spokesperson for the secretary of state’s office said in an email Wednesday.
Although the backlog related to the DPS records has been cleared, election officials continue to process voter registration applications they’re receiving by mail and in person ahead of the election. Even if they are processed later, registrations that were postmarked or submitted through DPS’ portal ahead of the Oct. 5 registration deadline will be considered valid for the Nov. 3 election.
Pierce said if a voter registered through the DPS web portal but does not appear on the voter roll, they can cast a provisional ballot and election officials will take additional steps to determine their eligibility so it can be counted.
“Election officials have an established method with DPS to check the transaction. If that voter did register through DPS, the vote will be counted,” she said.

sources.news_title: Texas resolves voter registration backlog ahead of 2026 midterms
sources.text:
Election officials in Texas faced a significant challenge as they worked to clear a backlog of over 593,000 voter registrations caused by a technical error in the state’s voter-registration system. This issue, emerging just before the early voting period, prompted a lawsuit from voting-rights groups against the Texas Department of Public Safety and the state’s Secretary of State, Robert H. “Hank” Sanders. The lawsuit seeks compliance with a 2021 settlement for a reliable online-registration system. As of October 14, county officials reported that the backlog was largely addressed, with assurances that affected voters could still cast provisional ballots if needed. The situation has emerged as a significant factor in the political landscape, particularly as Texas gears up for the critical midterm elections on November 3, 2026.
Key Takeaways
- Market analysis suggests that the backlog could influence Democratic turnout, potentially benefiting Gina Hinojosa in the gubernatorial race.
- The resolution of the voter registration issue before early voting appears to mitigate potential disruptions in the election process.
- Despite the technical error, the election infrastructure’s response may reassure voters about their ability to participate in the upcoming election.
What to Watch
Observers will be closely monitoring the impact of this registration backlog on voter turnout, particularly in Democratic-leaning counties like Harris, Dallas, and Travis. Any indication of a substantial increase in Democratic voter participation could be consistent with scenarios favoring Hinojosa. Additionally, attention will be on whether any further legal developments or technical issues arise that could affect voting procedures as the midterm elections approach. The resolution of these factors will be crucial in shaping the political dynamics in Texas leading up to November 3.
